The IOPAF assessment portal · v3.0 MVP

How good is your IT, really?

IOPAF is an assessment portal that answers that question with a number you can defend. Three business units — Development, IT Operations and Identity & Access Management — assess themselves in parallel, each against its own recognised standards, and every one of them lands on the same L0‑L5 ladder. Claims you cannot evidence are capped automatically, so the result reflects what you can show. Nothing leaves this browser.

Built on CMMI 14 standards in total — listed in full on the Standards page →

01
Why it exists

Most maturity scores are opinions. This one has to be earned.

Ask three teams how mature they are and you get three answers on three different scales, none of them auditable. IOPAF removes the argument: one rubric, one ladder, and a rule that an unevidenced claim is quietly marked down before it reaches any average.

MEASURE REALITY

Score what you can show, not what you believe

Ratings are evidence-gated. An unevidenced 4 or 5 counts one point lower, and follow-up questions only unlock where a foundation actually exists — so a confident answer with nothing behind it cannot lift the result.

ONE LANGUAGE, THREE UNITS

Development, Operations and IAM, directly comparable

Each unit is measured against the standards that genuinely apply to it, yet all three report on the same ladder. A development level, an operations level and a control-assurance level can sit side by side and be read as one picture.

FROM SCORE TO ACTION

A defensible level — and the road to the next one

Every result carries the reason it stopped where it did: the binding constraint, the weakest questions, and a roadmap stating exactly which criteria must improve and by how much to clear the next level.

REALITY CHECK → COMPARABLE MATURITY LEVELS → PRIORITIZED ACTION PLAN

04
The seven criteria

Every practice is judged on the same seven questions

Each criterion answers one plain question about the practice, and its weight sets how much it counts. Execution carries the most weight, because a process that is not actually practiced is not a process.

05
Why the number holds up

The level is capped, traceable and honest about coverage

A weighted average alone would let one strong criterion hide a broken one. Four hard caps prevent that, coverage rules stop half-finished work being reported as fact, and every question cites the clause it came from.

Four hard caps

The level starts from the weighted score, then these caps apply so averages cannot mask a weak dimension:

≤ L1the work is not consistently doneExecution < 1.5
≤ L2not standardized or staffedDef / People < 2.5
≤ L3performance is not measuredMeasurement < 3.5
≤ L4no working improvement loopImprovement < 4.0

Coverage, scope and provisional levels

Anything out of scope is excluded from every roll-up rather than scored as zero. A practice with less than 80% of its in-scope questions answered is reported as provisional — its level carries an asterisk and is left out of the confirmed organization level. If a capping criterion has no answers at all, the level cannot be confirmed.

Gap register and roadmap

For every assessed item: the binding constraint with the failing criterion and its score, the five weakest questions, and a roadmap naming the criteria that must improve and the score each must reach to clear the next level.

Every question is traceable

No question is invented for this platform. Each cites its origin — a specific practice on the development stream, practice guidance plus an institutionalization goal on operations, and the source control identifiers on the control stream — so any score can be defended line by line. Fourteen standards, three streams, one assessment instrument

IOPAF does not invent a standard: it composes published ones. Development is assessed against CMMI‑DEV v1.3, with TMMi v1.3 and ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 as testing deep-dives at Test & Verify. IT Operations pairs ITIL (Version 5) as the scope standard with CMMI‑SVC v1.3 as the depth standard. IAM control assurance consolidates eight control sources — ISO/IEC 27002:2022, ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A, NIST CSF 2.0, NIST SP 800‑53 R5, CIS Controls v8.1, SCF IAC, PCI DSS v4.0.1 and COBIT 2019 — into one 148-statement library. Optional overlays add ISO/IEC/IEEE 12207, ISO/IEC 25010, DORA and ISO/IEC 20000‑1. The figures below place every standard on the ideation→operation journey and show how they relate — then each is read on its own terms.

FIG. 01ASSESSMENT COVERAGE · IDEATION → OPERATION

Where each standard applies on the journey

Before reading the standards one by one, see them in context: the assessed journey runs from ideation to operation in nine stages, and each standard governs its part of that journey — development standards up to release, testing overlays at Test & Verify, operations standards from strategy through run-and-improve.

FIG. 02HOW THE STANDARDS FIT TOGETHER

One engine, three streams, all standards

Each stream pairs a scope standard (what to assess) with a depth standard (how well it is institutionalized), and can switch on optional overlays in Setup. Both streams feed the same IOPAF scoring engine, so a development team and an operations team produce directly comparable maturity levels.

FIG. 03CONTROL SOURCES · IAM STREAM

Seven external standards reduce to one 148-statement control library

The IAM stream is a consolidated control library, not a new standard. Each of the 148 statements carries its authoritative source citations, so a single assessment can be reported against ISO 27001/27002, NIST CSF and 800-53, CIS, SCF, PCI DSS and COBIT simultaneously. The counts below show how many statements cite each source — a statement usually cites two or three.

THE CRITERIA · STANDARD BY STANDARD What each standard actually measures — its own criteria set, explained separately before they are mapped together.
EDITION NOTES & QUESTION-LEVEL TRACEABILITY

Which editions are used, and how each question is cited

ITIL (Version 5) — January 2026 PeopleCert release

The edition in use reorganizes all 34 practices into 22 product & service management and 12 general management practices, introduces the eight-activity product & service lifecycle (Discover, Design, Acquire, Build, Transition, Operate, Deliver, Support), and elevates AI governance and digital experience to core quality characteristics. Question-level references point to that practice guidance, which is why the operations stream carries 34 practices rather than the earlier practice count.

CMMI-SVC v1.3 — the institutionalization spine

Generic goals GG2 (managed) and GG3 (defined) define what "managed" and "defined" mean at evidence level, and that is precisely what the seven IOPAF criteria operationalize. Process-area specific goals drive the Execution probes. The resulting capability logic is also consistent with the ITIL Maturity Model and with CMMI 3.0 practice areas, so results remain readable to assessors trained on either.

CMMI-DEV v1.3 and TMMi v1.3 — clause-level citation

Every execution probe on the development stream cites the exact specific practice — for example RD SP 3.5 or VER SP 2.1–2.3 — and each testing question cites its TMMi process area and specific goal, cross-referenced to ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 where the test documentation requirement is the governing one.

The control library — multi-source citation

Each of the 148 control statements retains the identifiers of every source that requires it, typically two or three of ISO/IEC 27002:2022, ISO/IEC 27001 Annex A, NIST CSF 2.0, NIST SP 800-53 R5, CIS Controls v8.1, SCF IAC and PCI DSS v4.0.1, with COBIT 2019 as the governance overlay. One test therefore satisfies several reporting obligations at once.

1

CMMI-DEV v1.3 — the development criteria

SCOPE + DEPTH · ONE MODEL OWNED BY · DEVELOPMENT UNIT

What it is. The development constellation of CMMI (SEI / ISACA) — a staged maturity model for organizations that build software and products. Its criteria come in two kinds: specific goals & practices per process area (what the discipline must do) and generic goals GG2/GG3 (how deeply any process must be institutionalized). IOPAF assesses its 12 process areas, organized in three groups:

ENGINEERING — 6 PROCESS AREAS
  • RD · Requirements Development — elicit, analyze, validate
  • REQM · Requirements Management — trace & control change
  • TS · Technical Solution — design, build, code standards
  • PI · Product Integration — assemble & verify interfaces
  • VER · Verification — peer reviews, testing vs requirements
  • VAL · Validation — does it work in the intended environment
PROJECT MANAGEMENT — 3
  • PP · Project Planning — estimates, plan, commitments
  • PMC · Project Monitoring & Control — track vs plan, act
  • RSKM · Risk Management — identify, analyze, mitigate
SUPPORT — 3
  • CM · Configuration Management — baselines, audits
  • PPQA · Process & Product QA — objective adherence checks
  • DAR · Decision Analysis & Resolution — formal alternatives

The depth criteria. The same model supplies institutionalization depth: GG2 — managed process (GP 2.1 policy · 2.2 plan · 2.3 resources · 2.4 responsibility · 2.5 training · 2.6 work-product control · 2.7 stakeholders · 2.8 monitor & control · 2.9 adherence evaluation · 2.10 management review) and GG3 — defined process (GP 3.1 tailored from the organizational standard · GP 3.2 improvement data collected).

WHAT IT CONTRIBUTES TO IOPAFThe full development stream: 12 process-area columns and the GG2/GG3 depth rows, assessed with the same seven criteria — 638 questions citing DEV specific practices (e.g. VER SP 2.1–2.3 peer reviews).
WHAT IT LEAVES TO OTHERSLive-service operations (ITIL V5 + CMMI-SVC) and the dedicated test-capability deep-dive (TMMi / ISO 29119). Pure operations organizations leave the stream switched off.
2

TMMi v1.3 — the testing criteria

TESTING DEEP-DIVE · OPTIONAL OVERLAY OWNED BY · DEVELOPMENT UNIT (TEST)

What it is. The Test Maturity Model integration (TMMi Foundation) — the testing counterpart of CMMI, built as a five-level staged model whose criteria are test-specific process areas gated per level. Paired with ISO/IEC/IEEE 29119 (test processes, documentation templates and design techniques) it forms IOPAF's Test & Verify yardstick:

TMMi L1
Initial
testing is ad hoc, part of debugging — no process areas
TMMi L2
Managed
test policy & strategy · test planning · test monitoring & control · test design & execution · test environment
TMMi L3
Defined
test organization · training program · lifecycle integration · non-functional testing · peer reviews
TMMi L4
Measured
test measurement · product quality evaluation · advanced reviews
TMMi L5
Optimizing
defect prevention · quality control · test process optimization
WHAT IT CONTRIBUTES TO IOPAFWhen selected in Setup, VER / VAL / PPQA are answered against TMMi’s goals and 29119’s documented processes — a dedicated test-capability audit whose five levels map one-to-one onto IOPAF’s L1–L5 ladder and drop straight into the same dashboard.
WHAT IT LEAVES TO OTHERSEverything outside testing: requirements, architecture and delivery stay with CMMI-DEV; live operations stay with ITIL V5 + CMMI-SVC. It never extends scope — it deepens Stage 06.
3

ITIL (Version 5) — the operations scope criteria

THE SCOPE · WHAT SHOULD BE HAPPENING OWNED BY · IT OPERATIONS UNIT

What it is. The world’s most widely adopted ITSM framework (PeopleCert, January 2026), reframing ITSM as Digital Product & Service Management. Its criteria are 34 practices — each with a purpose statement and success factors — flowing through an eight-activity lifecycle (Discover → Design → Acquire → Build → Transition → Operate → Deliver → Support):

PRODUCT & SERVICE MANAGEMENT — 22 PRACTICES
  • Core run: Incident · Service Request · Problem · Service Desk · Monitoring & Event
  • Change & release: Change Enablement · Release · Deployment · Service Validation & Testing
  • Design & assets: Service Design · Service Catalog · Service Configuration · IT Asset
  • Reliability: Service Level · Availability · Capacity & Performance · Service Continuity · Information Security
  • Platform & dev: Infrastructure & Platform · Software Development & Mgmt · Business Analysis · Service Financial
GENERAL MANAGEMENT — 12 PRACTICES
  • Direction: Strategy · Portfolio · Architecture · Risk
  • Improvement: Continual Improvement · Measurement & Reporting · Knowledge
  • People & partners: Workforce & Talent · Relationship · Supplier · Organizational Change · Project Management
WHAT IT CONTRIBUTES TO IOPAFThe column headers of the operations assessment: which 34 practices to assess, each practice’s purpose and success factors, and its lifecycle position. Every operational question cites its ITIL V5 practice guidance.
WHAT IT LEAVES TO OTHERSITIL has no scoring model — it cannot say how deeply a practice is embedded. That depth judgement is supplied by CMMI-SVC’s generic goals.
4

CMMI-SVC v1.3 — the operations depth criteria

THE DEPTH · HOW WELL IT MUST STICK OWNED BY · IT OPERATIONS UNIT

What it is. The services constellation of CMMI — a maturity model for service organizations whose core idea is institutionalization: a capability only counts if it survives staff turnover and pressure. Its criteria applied in IOPAF are the generic goals, identical for every practice:

GG2 — A MANAGED PROCESS (GP 2.1–2.10)
  • GP 2.1 organizational policy · GP 2.2 planned process
  • GP 2.3 adequate resources · GP 2.4 assigned responsibility
  • GP 2.5 trained people · GP 2.6 controlled work products
  • GP 2.7 stakeholders involved · GP 2.8 monitored & controlled
  • GP 2.9 adherence objectively evaluated · GP 2.10 management review
GG3 — A DEFINED PROCESS (GP 3.1–3.2)
  • GP 3.1 the process is tailored from an organizational standard process
  • GP 3.2 improvement information (measures, lessons) is collected and fed back
STAGED LEVELS — THE GATE RULE
  • ML1 Initial → ML2 Managed → ML3 Defined → ML4 Quantitatively Managed → ML5 Optimizing
  • You cannot claim a level while its gate is unmet — mirrored by IOPAF’s constraint caps
WHAT IT CONTRIBUTES TO IOPAFThe rows of the assessment: the seven criteria are a plain-language re-expression of GG2/GG3, the 0–5 scale mirrors the staged levels, and the four constraint caps replicate the gate rule.
WHAT IT LEAVES TO OTHERSCMMI-SVC is content-agnostic about which IT practices matter — it needs ITIL’s catalog for scope, just as GG2/GG3 need CMMI-DEV’s process areas on the development side.
5

Omantel IDM / User Access Management — the control criteria

CONTROL ASSURANCE · 7 SOURCE FRAMEWORKS OWNED BY · IDENTITY & SECURITY UNIT

What it is. A control library rather than a maturity model: 148 control statements that define what good identity and access management looks like in this organization, organized into 8 domains and 32 control groups. Each statement is traced to its authoritative source and carries the metadata an auditor needs — a weight, the tier of systems it applies to, the evidence tier required to claim it, a sample size, a test method and an accountable owner.

GOVERNANCE & LIFECYCLE — 4 DOMAINS
  • D1 · Governance & Policy — 14 controls · is IAM mandated, owned, measured
  • D2 · Identity Lifecycle — 24 controls · joiner, mover, leaver correctness
  • D3 · Authentication — 18 controls · MFA, session, credential strength
  • D4 · Roles & SoD — 22 controls · least privilege, toxic combinations
ASSURANCE & PLATFORM — 4 DOMAINS
  • D5 · Privileged Access — 20 controls · discovery, vaulting, session recording
  • D6 · User Access Review — 16 controls · recertification and revocation
  • D7 · Platform & Integration — 18 controls · connectors, provisioning, reconciliation
  • D8 · Assurance & Logging — 16 controls · evidence, monitoring, reporting
SOURCE FRAMEWORKS — SELECTABLE
  • ISO/IEC 27002:2022 & 27001 Annex A — control baseline
  • NIST CSF 2.0 — governance and outcome functions
  • NIST SP 800-53 R5 — federal control catalogue
  • CIS Controls v8.1 — prioritized safeguards
  • SCF — IAC domain · PCI DSS v4.0.1 · COBIT 2019

How IOPAF scores it. Each control is rated on the same 0–5 ladder (0 not implemented · 1 ad hoc · 2 partial · 3 implemented · 4 measured · 5 optimized), so a control level reads exactly like a practice level. Two rules keep it honest: an evidence gate — a rating at or above the control’s evidence tier is automatically capped unless the artefact has been seen at the stated sample size — and a weighted roll-up to control group, domain and stream, where high-weight controls (weight 3) count one-and-a-half times as much as standard ones.

WHAT IT CONTRIBUTES TO IOPAFA parallel control-assurance stream that answers “are our identity controls actually operating?” with auditable evidence, expressed in the same maturity language as the practice streams so the three results sit on one page.
WHAT IT LEAVES TO OTHERSIt says nothing about how well delivery or service-management practices are institutionalized — that remains CMMI-DEV, TMMi, ITIL V5 and CMMI-SVC territory. Controls test compliance; practices test capability.
HOW THE FOUR CRITERIA SETS MAP TO EACH OTHER The four practice standards converge on the same seven IOPAF criteria — first visually, then line by line — while the IAM control library is scored on the same 0–5 ladder through its own evidence-gated register.

Scale alignment: IOPAF L0–L5 ≡ CMMI ML1–ML5 (L2 ≈ GG2 achieved · L3 ≈ GG3 achieved) ≡ TMMi L1–L5 — which is why a TMMi-informed test rating and a CMMI-informed development rating drop into the same dashboard as directly comparable numbers.

How the standards work together

The engine multiplies breadth by depth for both streams: on the development stream CMMI-DEV supplies both — its 12 process areas as columns and its GG2/GG3 generic goals as rows; on the operations stream ITIL (Version 5) supplies the practice columns and CMMI-SVC the institutionalization rows. One scoring model, one rubric, one dashboard for two business units.

Criteria ↔ CMMI comprehensive mapping (DEV & SVC)

Each IOPAF criterion draws on the full CMMI constellation — CMMI-DEV on the development stream and CMMI-SVC on the operations stream — generic goals & practices (GG/GP — does the capability stick?), process areas with their specific goals & practices (PA · SG/SP — is the content right?), and the staged maturity levels the criterion gates. The highlighted ML chips show where each criterion primarily discriminates. Bar width = criterion weight in the composite score.

How to read this mapping — the notation explained

GG · GP
Generic Goals & Generic Practices — CMMI's institutionalization requirements that apply to every process. GG2 "Institutionalize a Managed Process" is met through practices GP 2.1–2.10 (e.g., GP 2.1 establish a policy, GP 2.5 train people, GP 2.8 monitor & control); GG3 "Institutionalize a Defined Process" adds GP 3.1–3.2 (tailor from an organizational standard, collect improvement data). In plain terms: does the capability stick, or does it evaporate when key people leave?
PA · SG
Process Areas with Specific Goals & Specific Practices — the content-specific requirements of each CMMI-SVC discipline. A PA (Process Area) is a cluster of related practices, cited by its acronym: IRP Incident Resolution & Prevention, SD Service Delivery, SCON Service Continuity, SST Service System Transition, MA Measurement & Analysis, PPQA Process & Product Quality Assurance, OPD/OPF/OPM Organizational Process Definition / Focus / Performance Management, OT Organizational Training, CAM Capacity & Availability Management, CM Configuration Management, REQM Requirements Management, SSD Service System Development, STSM Strategic Service Management, QWM/QPM Quantitative Work/Project Management, OPP Organizational Process Performance, CAR Causal Analysis & Resolution, IWM Integrated Work Management. Each PA contains numbered SGs (Specific Goals) achieved through SPs (Specific Practices). In plain terms: is the right content being done?
ITIL V5
ITIL (Version 5) anchor — the matching guidance in the January 2026 PeopleCert edition: the practice's purpose statement, practice success factors, and its position in the eight-activity Product & Service Lifecycle. ITIL defines what good operations look like; CMMI defines how deeply it must be institutionalized.
ML1–ML5
Maturity Level gates — CMMI's five staged maturity levels: ML1 Initial (work happens but is ad hoc and heroic), ML2 Managed (planned, resourced and tracked per practice), ML3 Defined (tailored from organization-wide standards), ML4 Quantitatively Managed (statistically measured and controlled), ML5 Optimizing (data-driven continual improvement). A highlighted chip means the criterion is the primary gate at that level — e.g., Measurement & Reporting is highlighted at ML4 because no organization can claim Level 4 without quantitative measurement, exactly mirroring IOPAF's cap rule Msr < 3.5 → ≤ L3.
